title: Hollywood Homicide
full_review:
Hollywood gets a bad reputation for churning out mindless cinematic junk, of which "Hollywood Homicide" (Columbia) is the latest example.

Name stars like Harrison Ford and Josh Hartnett will draw audiences initially, but director Ron Shelton is unable to meld this odd-couple, police procedural, action buddy comedy into satisfying movie entertainment.

It's supposed to be hilarious that Los Angeles police detectives Joe Gavilan (Ford) and K.C. Calden (Hartnett) pay as much attention to their moonlighting -- real estate for Joe, showbiz for K.C. -- as to catching killers. Unfortunately, the lame comedic situations and cliched dialogue seriously limit smiles and nearly preclude laughter.

Nor does character development fare any better. We learn K.C.'s cop father was mysteriously killed on the job, but when the killer is ultimately revealed the scene holds no emotional resonance. Likewise, we hear from a third party that Joe's had three wives and two children but from what we see of Joe they don't seem to exist.

Grizzled vet Joe and would-be actor K.C. are assigned to solve the quadruple murder of an up-and-coming rap group in a hip-hop club. But they are hard-pressed to follow up leads as Joe is desperate to broker a real estate deal for the commission payout, and K.C. is preoccupied giving yoga classes and planning a showcase of his acting talents. Yet they somehow find time for casual sex -- K.C. with a few of his yoga students, all of whom seem to be stunning twentysomethings, and Joe with an on-air radio psychic (Lena Olin).

Meanwhile, Joe's longtime enemy (Bruce Greenwood), now in Internal Affairs, is out to nail Joe however he can. And it seems all too dramatically convenient that Joe belatedly discovers his new lover is either his enemy's wife or girlfriend. The detectives' pursuit of sole eyewitness K-Ro (Karupt) and prime suspect, music mogul Sartain (Isaiah Washington), is often sidetracked as the cops juggle their off-duty hours between dames and deals.

The script, co-written by Shelton with former cop Robert Souza, wanders all over the lot to pump up the action and keep the pace moving. However, the effect is to confuse with extraneous characters and concerns that just fritter away by the conclusion. Here and there a cutely amusing moment surfaces, but more often the narrative is weighed down by drawn-out foot pursuits, car chases and shootouts that have been similarly filmed umpteen times before.

The sight of Ford sliding down an escalator banister isn't particularly funny, but then neither is this muddled movie.

Due to intermittent violence, implied casual affairs, a few racial epithets, frequent profanity and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
